# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

</document>
response:
# Review: *Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations*

This follow-up does several things right. The registered protocol carries forward, it adds a stricter hours measure (system logs), it pre-registers the mediation test, and it engages directly with the re-analysis and the meta-analysis. It reports a disappointing result plainly: the counter arm was ended. It also reports an unplanned observation that cuts against its own preferred story. And it describes the Halden survivors' figures as an upper bound rather than an estimate.

The core arithmetic checks out:

- **Output per hour, timesheets:** 0.966 / 0.88 = +9.8%
- **Output per hour, logs:** 0.966 / 0.89 = +8.5%
- **Halden subset:** 34.9 / 40.3 = −13.4%, and 96.8 / 0.866 = +11.8%
- **Mediation shares:** 47 + 18 + 35 = 100

Point 1 below is the most consequential: it affects the paper's headline estimate of decay.

---

## 1. The decay estimate is confounded by changes in control offices

In month 15, two of the seven control offices cut their own meetings. Their output per hour rose by about 4.1%. That raises the control arm's average by roughly 1.2% (4.1% × 2/7), which narrows the treated–control difference at 24 months by about a point.

So part of the reported decline from 12.5% to 9.8% (roughly 1 of the 2.7 points) may reflect the control arm improving, not the treatment effect fading. The paper treats the month-15 meeting audit as an aside about mechanism. It is also contamination of the comparison group, and it biases the decay estimate toward overstating fade.

**Needed:** a sensitivity analysis that excludes those two offices, or that ends the control comparison at month 15. Also, the audit happened after the nine-month report publicised the meetings finding. If the published result prompted it, say so; that would be a direct pathway of contamination.

---

## 2. Problems with the mediation analysis

**2a. "Confirms" is too strong.**
The Summary says the registered test "confirms" the meetings pathway. The Limitations, however, note that mediation assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediator and outcome, and that a cluster trial can't guarantee this. Meeting reduction was not randomised. Offices with more capable managers may have cut meetings *and* improved in other ways. Replace "confirms" with "is consistent with" or "supports."

**2b. This is not an independent replication.**
The hypothesis came from the same seven treated offices, and the 24-month data overlap the period that generated it. Registering at month 11 prevents analytic flexibility, which is valuable. It does not provide new units. "Survives a registered test" is accurate. Calling it a response to the charge that the original finding was a "post hoc story" overstates it, because a fresh sample would be needed to answer that charge.

**2c. The intervals look too narrow for 14 clusters.**
The 47% (28 to 66) and 18% (2 to 34) intervals rest on 7 v 7 offices. The phrase "a larger sample of office-months" suggests repeated measures may have been treated as independent. They aren't: the effective sample is still 14 offices. The paper needs to state how the intervals were computed, for example by cluster bootstrap at office level. The fatigue pathway (lower bound 2%) may not survive a small-cluster correction. My review of the nine-month report raised the same inference concern, and the follow-up doesn't say whether it was addressed.

**2d. The meetings pathway is partly an accounting identity.**
Meetings produce no closed cases. If meeting time counts in the hours denominator, removing about 3.3 hours of it raises output per hour almost automatically. The finding is still substantive, since it locates the gain in removing low-value time. But "47% explained" partly reflects how productivity is measured, not a behavioural mechanism.

**2e. What do the logs measure?**
The logs are described as recording "time staff are working on cases." If they capture only case work, the hours don't reconcile:
- Total hours fell by about 4.5 per week.
- About 3.3–3.5 of those were meetings.
- So case-working time should have fallen by only about 1 hour (around 3%), not 11%.

If instead staff remain logged in during meetings, the description is inaccurate, and point 2d applies with full force. In either case, the paper should state exactly what log time includes.

**2f. Where did the baseline data come from?**
- **Meetings:** The nine-month report said calendar data were collected *only in month six*. This report gives baselines of 7.4 hours (treated) and 7.2 hours (control).
- **Logs:** Log hours appear only at 24 months in Table 1, yet a difference-in-differences of −11% requires a pre-period.

Presumably both were extracted retrospectively from county systems. Say so, and confirm that the definitions match across periods.

**2g. A small inconsistency in control meeting time.**
Control meetings averaged 7.2 → 7.0 hours. Yet two of the seven control offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0. Taken together, these imply the other five control offices *increased* meeting time by about half an hour each. That's possible, but worth checking.

---

## 3. Comparisons and wording

**Like-for-like comparison in the Summary.**
"Fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months" sets a timesheet figure against a log figure. The body correctly uses 12.5% → 9.8% for the like-for-like comparison. The Summary should lead with that and give 8.5% as the stricter 24-month figure.

**"Declined by about a quarter."**
- 12.5% → 9.8% is a decline of about 22% on the raw percentages, or about 21% on the log scale. "About a fifth" is more accurate.
- If the log measure is used, 12.5% → 8.5% is about a third, but that comparison isn't like-for-like.
- Allowing for the contamination in point 1, true decay may be smaller than either figure.

**Characterisation of the re-analysis.**
"The gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy … had suggested." Varga & Holm extrapolated *energy* to baseline (at month ten by their account; about 8.7 on a straight-line reading) and argued that the residual gain should not be read as durable. They did not forecast output per hour reaching zero at month ten. The rebuttal holds without the sharper paraphrase. Quote them instead.

---

## 4. The Halden subset

**The marketing agency doesn't fit the "coverage" story.**
The Summary says all three reverters had "client-facing or coverage obligations." A marketing agency reverting because of *client deadlines* is deadline-driven work, which the meta-analysis would code as discretionary. Grouping it under "client-facing" stretches the category after the fact. It is a mild counterexample to the clean split between discretionary and coverage-bound work, and the paper should report it as one.

**The sample is selected three times, not twice.**
Organisations completed the pilot, continued the schedule, *and* agreed to respond: 14 of the 23 contacted (61%). Organisations that reverted or struggled may be the ones that declined to respond. The upper-bound framing is right, but the selection is stronger than the paper describes.

**Check the baseline hours.**
40.3 hours is the baseline Varga & Holm reported for the 27 organisations with time tracking. Confirm that it is the baseline for *these 11* organisations rather than a figure carried over.

**The earlier misreporting goes unaddressed.**
Okafor co-authors this report. The Halden working paper's description of its withdrawals ("during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons") was contradicted by the microdata. This follow-up would be a natural place to acknowledge or correct that, and it doesn't.

---

## 5. Smaller points

- **Uncertainty missing for secondary outcomes.** Sick days, resignations and appeal-overturn rates are reported without intervals at 24 months. Appeal overturn rates now have enough lag to be informative, so give them intervals.
- **Sick-day measurement.** Earlier reviews asked whether sick days were counted per day or per hour. This still isn't answered.
- **Basis for the counter-arm cost estimate.** The county estimated that restoring service would need 12% more staff and raise cost per contact by 9%. Presumably the difference reflects non-staff costs or the per-hour gain; state which.
- **Critique of the meta-analysis.** The point that all four long-follow-up studies were uncontrolled and used scheduled hours is fair and well documented. It confirms that the meta-analysis's conclusion about decay rested on its weakest studies.

---

## Overall

The main conclusion is well supported: in discretionary case-processing work, a per-hour gain of roughly 8–10% persists at two years under strict measurement, smaller than at nine months but clearly above zero. The finding that the counter arm was untenable is also clear.

The two claims that need tempering are:
1. **The size of the decay**, which is confounded by the meeting audit in two control offices.
2. **The strength of the mediation result**, given the same-sample replication, 14 clusters, and the accounting component of the meetings pathway.

Across the five documents, the picture has converged:
- **Halden** overstated the per-hour gain.
- **Varga & Holm** were right about why Halden's figures were inflated, but wrong to conclude that nothing remained.
- **The meta-analysis** got the size of the gain about right, but declared it durable before the evidence could show that.
- **This follow-up** supplies the first controlled long-run evidence on durability.

The main question still open is the one the authors themselves raise: whether removing meetings and other low-value time without reducing hours could capture much of the gain. Answering it needs a trial arm that reorganises work without cutting hours.
